This report delivers a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program and provincial/territorial research and development (R&D) tax regimes across Canada as of 2026.

Canada operates a dual-mechanism federal R&D tax incentive architecture under the Income Tax Act (ITA): first, an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction of allowable SR&ED expenditures via a dedicated tax pool under subsection 37(1); and second, an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), coupled with cash refundability provisions under section 127.1. Following landmark legislative amendments introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025—which received Royal Assent via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026—the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most significant expansion in over a decade. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the enhanced 35% refundable ITC expenditure limit doubled from $3 million to $6 million, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) widened from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15 million–$75 million three-year average revenue phase-out, and capital expenditures, shared-use-equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 were restored to program eligibility.

Concurrently, federal Budget 2026 proposed to expand the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026 to encompass regulatory and certification validation studies as well as intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses, while the CRA launched a modernized 8-week optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026. At the provincial level, Québec enacted a structural overhaul for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing its fragmented legacy R&D credits with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation – CRIC) at rates of 30% on the first $1 million above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess expenditures (including capital property and pre-commercialization activities). When combined with provincial top-ups in Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and the Yukon, combined federal-provincial R&D tax incentives can recover a substantial portion of eligible R&D labour and capital outlays, provided claimants navigate strict anti-stacking assistance reductions, specified employee caps, 18-month statutory filing deadlines, and the binding five-question judicial standard established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen.
1. Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Tax Incentives

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is the cornerstone of the Government of Canada's innovation and industrial productivity strategy. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada—which holds legislative responsibility for drafting tax policy under the Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR)—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which holds operational responsibility for technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and tax credit assessments—the program provides broad-based, sector-agnostic support to businesses conducting R&D in Canada. Unlike discretionary government grants that are constrained by fixed departmental budget envelopes and competitive application windows, the SR&ED program is an entitlement enshrined in federal tax statute: any taxpayer that satisfies the technical criteria of subsection 248(1), incurs allowable and qualified expenditures under sections 37 and 127, and files the prescribed forms containing prescribed information within the statutory reporting deadline under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) is legally entitled to the tax incentives.
Structurally, the federal SR&ED regime delivers two distinct yet interconnected statutory mechanisms that operate sequentially in a claimant's tax computation:

items: The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures: Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may accumulate allowable current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and eligible capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada into a dedicated expenditure pool. Unlike ordinary capital or developmental outlays that might otherwise require capitalization or amortization over multiple years, the Section 37 pool permits the taxpayer to deduct any amount up to the full positive balance of the pool against net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year. Any undeducted balance in the Section 37 pool does not expire; it carries forward indefinitely as a running pool to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year, subject only to loss restriction event rules upon an acquisition of control under subsection 37(6.1) (and with the exception of partnerships, which must deduct their entire pool balance in the current fiscal period under paragraph 96(1)(e.1)).

The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Regime: Pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit calculated as a statutory percentage—either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate—of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. The ITC is first applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce the taxpayer's federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. If an unclaimed ITC balance remains after reducing Part I tax to nil, qualifying claimants—specifically Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), sole proprietorships (individuals), and certain trusts—may claim a direct cash refund of all or a portion (100% or 40%) of the remaining ITC under section 127.1. Any non-refundable or unrefunded ITC balance may be carried back up to 3 prior taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable.

body.text: To prevent double taxation relief on the same dollar of expenditure, the Section 37 pool and the Section 127 ITC interact across consecutive taxation years. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC that is deducted against Part I tax payable or refunded in cash under section 127.1 in a given taxation year (Year 1) reduces the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year (Year 2). If the Year 2 deduction of the prior year's ITC causes the Section 37 pool balance to become negative at the end of Year 2, that negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for Year 2 pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA, resetting the Section 37 pool balance to nil for the start of Year 3 under paragraph 37(1)(c.1). Consequently, the federal SR&ED ITC is effectively brought into income in the taxation year following its utilization or refund.

body.text: 2. Legislative Evolution and the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Modernization Reforms

A rigorous audit of Canadian R&D claims requires tracking the precise effective dates of four consecutive waves of legislative, administrative, and proposed reform between 2024 and 2026: (1) Bill C-69 (Royal Assent on June 20, 2024); (2) the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 legislative package enacted under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent on March 26, 2026); (3) the CRA's administrative modernization and launch of Pre-Claim Approval (April 1, 2026); and (4) the proposed Budget 2026 commercialization and intellectual property expansion.
2.1 Bill C-69 (2024): The "Excluded Loan" Exception to Government Assistance

Prior to 2024, a major audit trap for Canadian technology and manufacturing corporations involved concessional or unconditionally repayable loans from government agencies, such as the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI). In Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196) and CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178, affirming 2021 TCC 57), the Federal Court of Appeal held that even unconditionally repayable government loans constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA whenever their interest rates or repayment terms were more favourable than strictly commercial debt, thereby reducing the borrower's qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar in the year advanced.

To rectify this disincentive, Parliament enacted Bill C-69, which received Royal Assent on June 20, 2024. Bill C-69 amended the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA by carving out an "excluded loan" as defined in subsection 12(11) of the ITA. Under this amendment, a bona fide loan from a government, municipality, or public authority that carries reasonable repayment terms (and is not a forgivable loan or grant) is no longer treated as government assistance and does not reduce the claimant's Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool or qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. This measure was made retroactive to January 1, 2020, applying to qualifying public loans made after December 31, 2019. Claimants whose post-2019 SR&ED claims were reduced by such loans are permitted to file amended tax returns with revised Forms T661 for any taxation year that is not statute-barred, provided no new SR&ED expenditures are introduced past the 18-month reporting deadline.
2.2 The 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

Following proposals announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 2024) and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted comprehensive statutory enhancements to the SR&ED program in Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Following Royal Assent, the CRA published updated versions of its core policies and prescribed forms between May and October 2026—including revised Form T661 (May 15, 2026), Form T1145 and Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures Policy and SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026).
The four pillars of the Bill C-15 reforms, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for capital/lease property acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024), are:

items: Doubling the Annual Expenditure Limit to $6 Million: For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure threshold eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising the maximum annual enhanced ITC from $1,050,000 (35% of $3M) to $2,100,000 (35% of $6M).

Broadening the CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out to $15M–$75M: For CCPCs, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range (calculated across the associated corporate group) expanded from the legacy $10 million to $50 million corridor to $15 million to $75 million.

Extending the 35% Enhanced Refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Public companies were historically restricted to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined in subsection 127(9) of the ITA—are eligible to earn the 35% enhanced ITC on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures, with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures. For ECPCs, the $6 million expenditure limit phases out linearly when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years is between $15 million and $75 million under subsection 127(10.6). In addition, CCPCs (or associated groups of CCPCs) may elect under subsection 127(10.32) to compute their expenditure limit under the ECPC three-year average revenue formula rather than the taxable capital formula.

Reinstating SR&ED Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs: Having been repealed between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (excluding land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings) were restored to both the Section 37 deductible pool (paragraph 37(1)(b)) and the Section 127 qualified expenditure definition. Concurrently, Parliament reinstated First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (allowing 25% of the capital cost of new equipment used more than 50% in SR&ED in each of the first two periods to earn ITCs) and Equipment Lease Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024.

body.text: 2.3 Budget 2026: Proposed Commercialization, Regulatory Validation, and IP Protection Expansion

In Budget 2026, the federal government proposed a structural expansion of the SR&ED program designed to bridge the gap between laboratory R&D and domestic commercialization, projected to deliver $930 million in additional federal tax support over five years ($25 million in 2026–27, $200 million in 2027–28, $245 million in 2028–29, $225 million in 2029–30, and $235 million in 2030–31). Under the proposal, which has not yet been enacted, for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026 the scope of eligible SR&ED activities and expenditures would be expanded in two areas:

items: Regulatory and Certification Requirements: The scope of eligible SR&ED activities would be expanded to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a new or improved product or process. To qualify, these regulatory and certification activities would have to directly relate to an underlying project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules. All expenditure categories eligible under standard SR&ED rules (salaries and wages, materials, subcontractor contracts, overhead, and machinery and equipment) could be claimed for these regulatory validation activities.

Intellectual Property (IP) Protection Expenditures: The scope of eligible SR&ED expenditures would be expanded to include costs reasonably incurred to obtain (register) and maintain IP protection in respect of IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Eligible IP forms would comprise patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software registered or protected under Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation. Covered outlays would include expenses to prepare and file IP applications, periodic maintenance fees payable to keep IP rights in force, and administrative fees payable to IP offices outside Canada. However, three strict exclusions would apply: (1) costs incurred to enforce or litigate IP rights (e.g., infringement lawsuits) would be excluded; (2) costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights would be excluded; and (3) supporting activities (such as patent drafting or application preparation) would be eligible only if conducted in Canada. Furthermore, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed for IP protection costs, recapture rules would apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and ITC amounts.

body.text: 3. Technical Eligibility Framework — Subsection 248(1), the "Why" and "How" Requirements, and Statutory Exclusions
3.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal threshold for technical eligibility across all federal and provincial R&D tax claims in Canada is governed by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (formerly located in section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations prior to its statutory relocation into the main body of the Act). Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of four qualifying limbs:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research seeks to expand the existing scientific knowledge base—often conducted by universities or research laboratories, as well as by businesses in fields such as biotechnology and nanotechnology—without targeting a specific commercial application.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research shares the knowledge-generation objective of basic research but directs the inquiry toward a defined practical goal, such as developing a vaccine by exploiting newly identified viral characteristics.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category in Canadian corporate filings. As emphasized by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, technological advancement does not require a revolutionary breakthrough; incremental, gradual improvements to existing materials, devices, products, or processes explicitly qualify under paragraph 248(1)(c).

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Support Work: Work with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories—namely engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. Support work does not constitute SR&ED on a standalone basis; its eligibility is strictly derivative of, and proportional to, the underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development project.

body.text: 3.2 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 and the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Requirements

The administrative framework used by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) to evaluate subsection 248(1) has evolved through four historical stages, though the underlying statutory definition has remained constant:

items: Pre-1985 (Interpretation Bulletin IT-439) and the May 1985 Budget Papers: Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which proved insufficient to explain eligible research and development. In the May 23, 1985 Securing Economic Renewal Budget Papers tabled by Finance Minister Michael H. Wilson, the Department of Finance amended the regulatory definition to explicitly incorporate "experimental development" while excluding routine engineering and routine development.

Information Circular 86-4 (1986) and IC 86-4R3 (1994): Co-developed by Revenue Canada and industry leaders in 1986 and revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994 (following a March 4, 1986 Department of Finance clarification and Government of Canada News Release 92-088 on December 2, 1992), this circular established the classic three essential criteria: (i) Scientific or technological uncertainty, (ii) Scientific or technological advancement, and (iii) Scientific and technical content (systematic investigation).

The Five Questions ( Northwest Hydraulic , 1998, and the 2012/2015 Policy): In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839), Judge Bowman synthesized IC 86-4R3 and the statutory text into five foundational questions. The CRA formally adopted these five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in August 2021).

The August 2021 Guidelines ("Why" and "How" Requirements): In Summer 2021 (updated August 13, 2021), the CRA replaced the 2015 policy with the modernized Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, consolidating the five questions into Two Core Requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement.

body.text: Both requirements must be satisfied concurrently for a project to qualify:
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty & Advancement)
The "Why" requirement asks: Is the work conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement?

The CRA Guidelines distinguish between discovering conceptual knowledge (explanatory theories or prediction models—which qualifies) and merely gathering factual knowledge (measurements or data—which does not qualify). New scientific or technological knowledge is required when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge (defined as the combination of publicly available sources and internal business resources). Indicators of technological uncertainty in experimental development include: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; too many variables or unknowns exist; parameters or conditions are outside of normal operating ranges; the nature of the problem is evolving; data is not readily available; or there are interlocking constraints.

Circumventing a technological uncertainty via a workaround using existing available knowledge, or acquiring available knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge, does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement. Similarly, cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, although trying to meet cost targets might create technological uncertainty. Finally, whether a project succeeds or fails in achieving its objectives is irrelevant when assessing whether the work meets the "Why" requirement; only the purpose of the work matters. Rejecting a hypothesis through experimentation is still an advancement because it eliminates a previously untested hypothesis.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)
The "How" requirement asks: Is the work a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis?
Carrying out work systematically using established standards is not enough on its own. Instead, a systematic investigation or search includes four operational phases:

items: Generating an Idea (Hypothesis): Formulating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach).
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the idea to evolve and change as a result of testing.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis.
Keeping Evidence: Retaining evidence that is generated as the work progresses.

body.text: 3.3 Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)) and Distinguishing Support Work
Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial and routine activity from the definition of SR&ED:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes;
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;

Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas (note that a business conducting SR&ED while prospecting for minerals may claim its eligible SR&ED work, but must exclude the work with respect to prospecting for minerals);
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;

Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes (note that in Québec, product design involving development of form and aesthetics may qualify under the separate pre-commercialization component of the provincial CRIC); and
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA Guidelines emphasize, purpose is the decisive factor that distinguishes eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) from excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k). If data collection or testing is conducted for routine business operations (such as normal quality control or quality assurance), it is excluded. Conversely, if data collection or testing is performed specifically to directly support eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as eligible SR&ED work; under the Budget 2026 proposal, work to satisfy initial regulatory certification requirements directly related to an eligible SR&ED project would also qualify for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), the Section 37 Deductible Pool, and Traditional vs. Proxy Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method: Election Mechanics and Strategic Trade-Offs

Under subsection 37(10) and clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) of the ITA, a claimant must select one of two statutory methodologies on Form T661 (Part 3, Section A, lines 160 and 162) to compute its SR&ED expenditures for each taxation year:

items: The Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) & ITR Subsection 2900(4)): The claimant elects not to track or claim specific SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED "salary base" (subject to the overall cap on the PPA under ITR subsection 2900(6)). The PPA is added to "qualified expenditures" on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn federal (and applicable provincial) ITCs. However, the PPA is not added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant deducts its actual overhead outlays (utilities, office supplies, clerical wages, employer share of related benefits) as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the ITA.

The Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) & ITR Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)): The claimant specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures incurred in the taxation year that are All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) attributable or directly attributable (meaning both directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. These actual overhead expenditures are reported on Line 360 of Form T661 and are included in both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes.

body.text: Critical Election Rules: The choice between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is made on a year-by-year basis on Form T661. If a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661 when the claim is filed, the CRA automatically processes the claim using the Traditional Method by default. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year.

body.text: 4.2 Detailed Eligibility Rules by Expenditure Category
1. Salaries and Wages & The Specified Employee Regime

Under subsection 248(1) and sections 5 to 8 of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment (which could relate to gross wages reported on a T4 slip for the calendar year if the tax year ends at the calendar year-end). For regular (non-specified) employees, allowable SR&ED salaries and wages include basic salary and wages, paid vacation, statutory holidays, regular sick leave, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, inducements/non-competition payments, and taxable benefits (both cash outlays and reasonable non-cash benefits net of GST/HST/PST unless no input tax credit can be claimed, provided the underlying cost is not also claimed as a business expense), multiplied by the percentage of time the employee spent on directly engaged SR&ED tasks. Directly engaged tasks include hands-on experimentation and analysis, the eight support work categories under paragraph 248(1)(d), certain non-specialized tasks (such as operating an experimental machine or feeding raw materials into a machine when supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications), first-line technical supervision of SR&ED employees, technological planning and feasibility studies for ongoing claimed projects, and internal technical documentation.

Salaries and wages never include the employer's share of related statutory or group benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, pension/insurance plans), extended vacation or extended sick leave, stock option benefits under section 7, retiring allowances, or shareholder dividends. Furthermore, in a partnership, a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership; any salary or wages paid to a partner is considered a distribution of income and cannot be claimed.

The Specified Employee Restrictions: Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (for example, a sister, brother, or spouse of a specified shareholder). Three strict statutory restrictions apply to specified employees:

items: Total Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Pay (ITA Subsection 37(9)): Any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap of 5 Times YMPE (ITA Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed for a specified employee in a taxation year cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee: Maximum Direct SR&ED Salary (Specified Employee) = 5 × YMPE × (Days in Tax Year ÷ 365)

Proxy Salary Base Cap of Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 Times YMPE (ITR Subsection 2900(7)): When computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661 (lines 852–858), taxable benefits (section 6), stock options (section 7), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages (section 78) are excluded for all employees under ITR subsection 2900(9). According to the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy and accounting guide CloudAcc, for each specified employee, the maximum salary that can enter the proxy salary base under ITR subsection 2900(7) is capped at the lesser of:
Actual directly engaged SR&ED salary (Column 4, Line 856);
75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits, Line 852); and

2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (Column 5, Line 858): Maximum Proxy Salary Base (Specified Employee) = 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365) where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days employed in the year.

body.text: Note that under ITR subsection 2900(6), the total Prescribed Proxy Amount for a business is also subject to an overall cap on the PPA calculated using the formula A − B − C, where A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), and B and C subtract specific deductions identified by the Regulations (such as capital cost allowance, the SR&ED deduction on line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, building rent, and interest).

If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the specified employee salary cap and proxy salary base cap must be allocated across the associated group by filing prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) pursuant to subsections 37(9.2)–(9.4) and ITR subsection 2900(8).

body.text: 2. Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (10% Cap)

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA, a claimant may include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work physically performed outside Canada (reported on Form T661 Line 307 for regular employees and Line 309 for specified employees, with project indicator Line 265) only if five cumulative conditions are met:

items: The foreign SR&ED work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not a contractor;
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The work was related to a business of the claimant;
The foreign work was an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; and
The salary or wages paid were not subject to an income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.5), as noted in the Practitioner's Income Tax Act and CPA Alberta CRA Roundtable guidance, this permissible foreign salary limit is calculated as 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages carried on in Canada. Separately, current expenditures for SR&ED performed outside Canada that do not qualify as permissible salaries can be deducted in computing net business income under subsection 37(2), but cannot be claimed on Form T661 and do not earn ITCs.
3. The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

items: Unpaid Remuneration (ITA Subsection 78(4)): Any salary, wages, or other employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year (identified on Line 315 of Form T661) is considered not incurred in that taxation year for both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 ITC purposes. If paid after 180 days, it can only be included as SR&ED salary for the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (Line 310 of Form T661), and under ITR subsection 2900(9) it can never be included in the proxy salary base.

Unpaid Non-Salary Current Expenditures (ITA Subsection 127(26)): Current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials, subcontracts, or overhead) that are incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of year-end remain included in the Section 37 deductible pool in the year incurred, but must be deducted from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes on Line 520 of Form T661. Crucially, unpaid amounts must be properly identified on Form T661 within 12 months after the filing-due date (18 months after the tax year-end for corporations); unpaid amounts not identified within this timeframe can never be included in calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures, even if paid later. When an arm's length contract expenditure remains unpaid past 180 days, a 20% reduction is made first and the remaining 80% is deducted as an unpaid amount; when subsequently paid in a later taxation year, 80% of the identified amount paid is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures.

body.text: 4. Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (ITA Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) & ITR Paragraph 2900(2)(a))

Per the Materials for SR&ED Policy, eligible materials must be physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object at a given moment in the SR&ED process (either an object on which SR&ED is carried out or an object that results from SR&ED). Materials are valued at their laid-down cost (including invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and reasonable costs or external services—such as galvanizing a metal part—required to bring the item to its required condition and location for SR&ED; or for internally manufactured inventory, laid-down material cost plus direct labour and production overhead under GAAP / IT-473R). When materials are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the actual cost can be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure, but under subsection 127(11.6) the ITC earned is limited to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier (excluding any profit mark-up). Purchased materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are physically consumed or transformed:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless (absorbed, used up, or disposed of as waste) as a result of SR&ED. While broken lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas used for ambient heating or plant cleaning) do not qualify as materials consumed, process water or energy/fuel sources that are integral to the chemical/physical conversion reaction under SR&ED investigation qualify if properly identified and documented.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Materials that are changed, physically altered, or incorporated into another material or tangible object (such as a custom product, experimental production run, or commercial asset) that retains some value or utility to the claimant or another party. Costs relating to excess production beyond what is required for SR&ED must be excluded. When transformed materials are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC Recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (36) apply.

body.text: 5. Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Traditional Method (ITR Paragraph 2900(2)(c) & Subsection 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method (reported on Line 360 of Form T661), overhead and other expenditures must either be All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) attributable to SR&ED or satisfy two cumulative tests under ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c):

items: The Directly Related Test: There must be a direct linkage—without an intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred.

body.text: Specific CRA overhead rules under the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy include:

items: Clerical & Administrative Staff: Salaries of clerical and administrative staff (e.g., HR, accounting, purchasing) providing a service to SR&ED employees qualify on Line 360 only to the extent there is a direct linkage and the cost is incremental. However, the employer's share of related benefits, travel, training, and retiring allowances for clerical/administrative staff are disallowed because their linkage to SR&ED work is indirect.

Telephones, Cellular Phones, and Internet: Fixed monthly subscription payments for telephone, cellular phone, or Internet services are considered ordinary fixed business expenses that fail the incremental test and are not allowable as SR&ED overhead regardless of the percentage of time spent on SR&ED. Only identifiable incremental charges (such as specific long-distance telephone charges directly tied to SR&ED) may qualify.

Travel, Training, Utilities, and Clinical Volunteers: Incremental utilities, travel and lodging in Canada to conduct testing at a customer location, training in Canada for hands-on SR&ED employees, fees paid to volunteers participating in clinical studies, and health/safety expenses directly linked to SR&ED may qualify on Line 360.

Prescribed Expenditures Excluded from ITCs (ITR Paragraph 2902(a), Line 530): Even if directly related and incremental, certain prescribed expenditures are barred by ITR paragraph 2902(a) from being included in qualified expenditures and cannot earn ITCs: (i) fees for preparing SR&ED claims; (ii) costs to attend conventions or conferences; (iii) interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g); (iv) legal or accounting fees; (v) entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses; (vi) dues or memberships in scientific/technical societies; and (vii) fines or penalties. Furthermore, no deduction or ITC is allowed under subsection 37(4) and ITR paragraph 2902(c) for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED.

body.text: 6. Contract Expenditures for SR&ED and Third-Party Payments (The 80% Inclusion Rule)

items: Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (ITA Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), Line 340): Payments to arm's length contractors who perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant (where the payer controls the work, retains exclusive IP rights, and accounts on an accrual basis; contractor details reported on lines 267–269) are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80% eligible for federal ITCs under paragraph (g) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) (20% is subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661). To earn ITCs, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier"; payments to non-taxable suppliers are stripped out on Line 528. Furthermore, the CRA applies a "look-through" rule to verify that the contracted work was performed in Canada and that the contract expenditure is reduced by any related expenditure of the performer that is not of a current nature.

Non-Arm's Length (NAL) Contracts: Payments to a non-arm's length performer for SR&ED are included in the calculation of deductible expenditures, but do not qualify for an ITC. Instead, qualified expenditures can be transferred between NAL performers and payers using prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) (with the performer reporting the agreed transferred amount on Line 540 of Form T661; note that if the performer attempts to transfer more than its qualified expenditure balance would otherwise have been, the Act states that no amount can be transferred).

Third-Party Payments (ITA Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) & (ii), Line 370, Form T1263): Payments made to an eligible third-party entity (Categorized as Entity A: Canadian resident corporations, accounted on an accrual basis; Entity B: approved associations; Entity C: approved universities, colleges, or research institutes; Entity D: non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j); Entity E: approved granting councils; and Entity F: paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations for basic/applied research) where the performer controls the R&D, rights are non-exclusive (generally published) with preferential exploitation rights for the payer, and tax treatment is generally on a cash basis (except Entity A). Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for ITCs (20% deducted on Line 529), and require completing and attaching Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.

body.text: 7. Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025), three classes of capital and equipment outlays incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify for SR&ED tax incentives:

items: ASA Capital Expenditures (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390): Expenditures to acquire new or used depreciable property (available for use after December 15, 2024) where the claimant's intention at acquisition is either (i) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time (including setup and changeover time) in its expected useful life in SR&ED in Canada, or (ii) to consume 90% or more of its value in SR&ED in Canada. Land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e). Qualifying ASA capital expenditures are 100% added to the Section 37 deductible pool (and must not be included on Schedule 8, Capital Cost Allowance, T2SCH8, unless the claimant fails to claim them on Form T661 by the reporting deadline) and 100% included in qualified expenditures for ITCs. Claimants must list the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties per project on Line 262 of Part 2 of Form T661 and the 20 most expensive properties overall in Box 780.

Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (ITA Subsection 127(9), Line 504 & Box 788): New depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA criterion, is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP—equipment intended at acquisition to be used during assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial plant/line and intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its useful life under ITR subsection 2900(11)). If the equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later), 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost (calculated without borrowed money costs under section 21 or deemed capital costs under subsection 13(7.4), and after non-arm's length adjustments under subsection 127(11.6)) is deemed a qualified expenditure as First-Term SUE. If actual SR&ED usage remains more than 50% of operating time through the Second Period (ending at the end of the first taxation year at least 24 months after acquisition), a further 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost qualifies as Second-Term SUE. SUE capital costs are not part of the Section 37 pool; they are depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule 8, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent year.

Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024): Under the Traditional Method, equipment used 90% or more (ASA) of operating time in SR&ED is 100% claimable as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), while equipment used less than 90% is claimable proportionally on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method, equipment (excluding GPOEF) used 90% or more of operating time is 100% claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), equipment used more than 50% to less than 90% ("primarily") is 50% claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and equipment used 50% or less is 0% claimable. Building rent is excluded under both methods except for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under ITR section 2903. Lease costs for structures (such as bridges or dams) or land (under the Traditional Method as overhead) may qualify if statutory tests are met. For a taxation year that straddles December 16, 2024, SR&ED equipment usage is calculated as a percentage of total operating time after December 15, 2024.

5.2 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Reduction Rules

items: Legacy CCPC Rules (Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024): For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only CCPCs qualified for the 35% enhanced rate, up to a maximum expenditure limit of $3,000,000. Under subsection 127(10.2), the $3 million expenditure limit began to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and any associated corporations) for the previous taxation year reached $10 million, and became nil starting at $50 million (using variable A, which is nil if prior-year taxable capital is less than or equal to $10 million, and otherwise is the lesser of $40 million and the amount by which taxable capital exceeds $10 million). (Note: Prior to the 2019 Federal Budget, the formula also included a reduction based on previous-year taxable income, which was repealed in 2019).

Enacted Post-Reform CCPC Taxable Capital Rules (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024): Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's maximum expenditure limit is $6,000,000. The expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year (across the associated group) reaches $15 million, and becomes nil starting at $75 million. Associated CCPCs must allocate this shared expenditure limit among group members using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3). Short taxation years and having multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year also reduce the expenditure limit.

Enacted ECPC (and Electing CCPC) Revenue-Based Rules (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024): For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—and for CCPCs or associated CCPC groups that file an election under subsection 127(10.32)—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced under subsection 127(10.6) when the corporation's (or consolidated/associated group's) average annual revenue reflected in its financial statements over the preceding 3 fiscal years (with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales of goods or services so that the annual revenue reflects a single economic entity) exceeds $15 million, and becomes nil starting at $75 million.

body.text: 5.3 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Pursuant to subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, a property on which it previously claimed an SR&ED ITC—specifically (1) materials for SR&ED included in a custom product, commercial asset, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development, (2) ASA capital equipment, (3) Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), (4) animals and other growing things used in SR&ED projects, or (5) property (other than IP) acquired through an SR&ED contract—the claimant must add back the recaptured ITC to its federal Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion.

Crucial distinction under subsection 127(32) ("meaning of cost"): if a claimant manufactures an SR&ED component or inventory item in-house, recapture applies only to the laid-down cost of the purchased materials originally acquired (there is no recapture on the internal manufacturing or SR&ED salaries or overhead incurred to build the item). Conversely, if the claimant orders a part from an arm's length supplier for $12,000 ($10,000 manufacturing and development cost plus a $2,000 profit element), the entire $12,000 cost of the property is subject to the recapture rules. Regarding intellectual property (IP) under an SR&ED contract: if IP rights rest with the payer from the outset, the payer has not acquired property from the performer and is not subject to recapture if it sells or leases the IP; if the payer pays a separate sum at the end of the project to purchase the IP rights from the performer, that IP purchase payment is not an allowable SR&ED expenditure. (Note that under the Budget 2026 proposal, if SR&ED support is claimed for IP protection registration/maintenance costs, recapture rules would apply upon disposition of that IP). Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year (or partnership excess recapture added to a partner's Part I tax under subsection 127(30)) increases the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3).
6. Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Statutory Reduction Rules (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(9), 127(18)–(20))

A foundational principle of the Canadian SR&ED system is that tax incentives are provided on the claimant's net costs of performing SR&ED in Canada. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the ITA, both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (reported on Form T661 lines 429–431) and the Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes must be reduced on an accrual, project-by-project basis by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of the SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year:

items: Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)): Any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, except where explicitly excluded by provincial statute for provincial calculations), investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a government, municipality, or public authority (including Crown corporations and foreign governments)—excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself and, retroactive to January 1, 2020 under Bill C-69, excluding bona fide public loans with reasonable repayment terms ("excluded loans" under subsection 12(11)). Common programs that constitute government assistance include NRC IRAP contributions, Mitacs awards, NSERC Alliance grants, and Ontario Centre of Innovation (OCI) Vouchers.

Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Any amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) received as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance for property cost or an outlay/expense.

Contract Payments (Subsection 127(9)): An amount paid or payable for SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of another person. When the amount of assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceeds the SR&ED expenditures of that project, the qualified SR&ED expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's length party for that project are reduced to nil (and excess assistance is carried forward to reduce qualified expenditures of that project in subsequent years, while excess assistance beyond the Section 37 pool is included in income).

body.text: When assistance is received by a member of a non-arm's length group whose total group qualified expenditures on the project exceed the assistance, the parties may allocate the assistance among group members by filing prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20). Conversely, if a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED claim, the repayment is added to the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earns an ITC in the year of repayment at the historical ITC rate that would have been earned in the year the assistance or contract payment was received.

7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes — Comprehensive Cross-Jurisdictional Analysis

Every Canadian province and territory—with the explicit exception of Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories (NWT), and Nunavut, which do not offer an R&D tax credit—maintains a dedicated R&D tax incentive program. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by the Province of Alberta), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through the federal T2 / T1 return system and harmonize their technical definition of eligible R&D with subsection 248(1) of the federal ITA. To qualify in any jurisdiction, the taxpayer must maintain a permanent establishment in that province or territory and physically carry out the SR&ED within that jurisdiction.
7.1 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul, Legacy Credits, IDCI Patent Box, and CDAE

Québec operates an autonomous innovation tax system administered by Revenu Québec, while harmonizing its scientific definition of basic research, applied research, and experimental development with federal legislation and relying on the CRA to carry out the scientific review.
1. The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Post-March 25, 2025)

As confirmed by the Ministère des Finances du Québec and Revenu Québec, for a taxation year beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec offers the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization ( Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation – CRIC):

items: CRIC Rates of Financial Assistance (Refundable):

30% on the portion of qualified expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, up to a maximum of $1,000,000 (associated corporations allocate this $1,000,000 expenditure limit using Form RD-1029.8.EN-T); and
20% on qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 maximum.
Applicable Exclusion Threshold: Qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an exclusion threshold corresponding to the greater of:
$50,000; or

The sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system for each employee (adjusted to reflect the actual time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities).
CRIC Qualified Expenditures: Eligible expenditures incurred by the corporation (or on its behalf) for R&D or pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec include:
Salaries or wages paid to the corporation's employees;
50% of the amount paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec;
50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, an eligible research consortium, or an eligible university entity; and

Property acquisition costs (excluding costs relating to the acquisition of a building, land, or a right to use a building or land). Any government or non-government financial assistance received for R&D or pre-commercialization expenses must be subtracted from qualified expenditures.

Single Tax Credit / Non-Cumulation Rules: A corporation cannot benefit from both the CRIC and another tax credit under the Québec tax system for the same expenditure. Specifically, a corporation cannot claim the CRIC for the acquisition of property if it claims the Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation (C3i) for that property (and vice versa), nor can a corporation holding an initial qualification certificate for the tax holiday for a large investment project claim the CRIC for property used or acquired for that project.
Eligible Pre-Commercialization Activities: Pre-commercialization activities must be undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec and include:
Tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation;
Product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials); and
Quality control activities only if related to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification.

Prescribed CRIC Forms: To claim the CRIC, an eligible corporation must complete Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)), alongside Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (for the pre-commercialization component) and Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (associated corporation expenditure limit agreement), and attach it to its corporate income tax return.

body.text: 2. Legacy Québec R&D Credits (Taxation Years Beginning Before March 26, 2025)

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning before the CRIC effective date (detailed in Revenu Québec document IN-109-V, Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development), Québec's legacy refundable R&D credits included:

items: Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D): Claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V (with Form RD-1029.7.8-T for associated corporations' expenditure limit agreement and Form RD-222-V, Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures), subject to an exclusion threshold of $50,000 that increased linearly for prior-year total assets between $50 million and $75 million up to $225,000.

Other Legacy Credits: Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, requiring a qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy), and Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V).

body.text: 3. Québec Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI)

To encourage the retention and valorization of Québec innovations, the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) (Form CO-737.18.CI) allows a corporation with an establishment in Québec to benefit from an effective corporate income tax rate of 2% on the qualified portion of its taxable income derived from commercializing a qualified intellectual property asset—representing a reduction of 9.5 percentage points from the general Québec corporate tax rate of 11.5%. Qualified IP assets comprise an invention protected by a patent or a certificate of supplementary protection, software protected by copyright, or a plant variety protected by a plant breeder's rights certificate resulting from R&D activities carried out in whole or in part in Québec. Qualified gross income includes income from selling or leasing property incorporating the asset, supplying a service intrinsically related to the asset, royalties, or judicial damages relating to the asset. The IDCI deduction is calculated using parameters A (net income for tax purposes), B (gross income from commercializing the IP asset), C (total gross income), D (estimate of profit not attributable to the IP asset), E (qualified R&D expenditures related to the IP asset and Québec), F (overall R&D expenditures related to the IP asset), and factor G = (11.5% − 2%) / 11.5% = 0.826 (82.6%).
4. Québec Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE / CDAE-IA)

Corporations carrying on an information technology business in Québec that hold annual qualification certificates from Investissement Québec for both their eligible activities and each eligible employee may claim the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE) by filing Form CO-1029.8.36.DA (within 12 months after the CO-17 filing due date or 3 months after certificate issuance). Industry funding analyses from Canadian Funding Partners note that while online summaries historically cited a fixed 24% refundable and 6% non-refundable split, recent Québec budget updates for CDAE / CDAE-IA introduced sliding scale rates, an exclusion threshold, and an artificial intelligence (AI) integration requirement.
7.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC (Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario))
Ontario provides three corporate R&D tax credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario):

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96, Schedule 566 / T2SCH566):

Rate & Cap: 8% refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (10% before June 1, 2016) on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short tax years), yielding a maximum annual tax credit of $240,000.

Phase-Out Thresholds: The $3 million expenditure limit is gradually reduced if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Capital Expenditure Restoration: Per Ontario's official program update (updated October 30, 2026), OITC qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures, 40% of qualified capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014, and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (excluding capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024).
Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Section 39, Schedule 508 / T2SCH508):

Rate & Scope: 3.5% non-refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (4.5% before June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reported on Schedule 5 line 416). Includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024.

Interaction with OITC, Carryover, Waiver & Recapture: The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) is a form of government assistance that reduces eligible expenditures for the ORDTC. Unused ORDTC may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, and a corporation may waive the current-year ORDTC in whole or in part under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). Recapture of ORDTC is calculated on Schedule 508 using the 23.56% rate and entered on Schedule 5 line 277.
Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569 / T2SCH568 & T2SCH569):

Rate & Cap: 20% refundable tax credit on qualified monetary payments (capped at $20,000,000 annually, for a maximum annual tax credit of $4,000,000) incurred under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—including Ontario universities, community colleges, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, or federal Networks of Centres of Excellence operating in Ontario—provided the corporation is not "connected" to the ERI (i.e., the ERI does not own shares carrying >10% of voting rights or >10% of fair market value, is not a partner, and deals at arm's length). Small businesses may claim both the 20% OBRITC and the 8% OITC on qualified expenditures.

body.text: 7.3 Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

items: British Columbia ( Income Tax Act (British Columbia) , Part 6, Sections 97–103, Form T666): Offers a 10% refundable credit (Section 98, Schedule 5 line 674) for qualifying CCPCs (and, for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs)) up to the lesser of their qualified BC expenditures and their expenditure limit ($6M x 10% = $600,000 maximum refundable credit for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024; previously $3M x 10% = $300,000), and a 10% non-refundable credit (Section 99, Schedule 5 line 659) for other non-CCPCs and expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit. For tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, B.C. also restored the eligibility of capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures and raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out so that the expenditure limit is eliminated at $75 million. Unused non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and forward 10 years, and may be renounced under subsection 100(1). Form T666 must be filed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year, and B.C. Budget 2026 made the credit permanent, removing the former September 1, 2027 end date. Recapture applies if property is disposed of or converted to commercial use within 10 years of acquisition (sections 102.1–102.6, Schedule 5 line 241).

Alberta ( Alberta Corporate Tax Act , Sections 26.95–26.99, AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970): Administered by the Province of Alberta (Information Circular IEG-1), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending. The grant provides an 8% payment for eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending (the average qualifying R&D spending over the previous 2 years), and a 20% payment for eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level. As noted by tax advisory firm TLedgers, the IEG phases out between $10 million and $50 million of taxable capital. The filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

Saskatchewan ( The Saskatchewan Income Tax Act, 2000 , Sections 63–63.4, Schedule 403 / T2SCH403): Offers a 10% R&D tax credit. Per the CRA's T4012 T2 Corporation Income Tax Guide, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs are eligible for a 10% refundable tax credit on the first $2,000,000 of eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (increased from the first $1,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; Schedule 5 line 645). Expenditures exceeding the CCPC refundable threshold, as well as eligible expenditures incurred by non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Schedule 5 line 631), subject to a yearly maximum credit limit of $1,000,000 for combined refundable and non-refundable credits. Unused non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and forward 10 years, and may be renounced under subsection 63.4(13).

Manitoba ( The Income Tax Act (Manitoba) , Section 7.3, Schedule 380 / T2SCH380): Provides a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible Manitoba expenditures. For in-house R&D, 50% of the tax credit is refundable (7.5% refundable on Schedule 5 line 613) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5% non-refundable on Schedule 5 line 606). If the eligible R&D is carried on in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute, the 15% credit is 100% (fully) refundable. Manitoba includes capital expenditures for depreciable property (excluding buildings) and first- and second-term SUE, and allows 100% (rather than 80%) on contracts with eligible Manitoba educational institutions. Unused non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and forward 20 years, and may be renounced under subsection 7.3(7). Eligible expenditures must be identified no later than 12 months after the corporate income tax return is due.
Atlantic Provinces (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador): All three participating Atlantic provinces provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit:

Nova Scotia ( Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia) , Section 41, Schedule 340 / T2SCH340): 15% fully refundable (Schedule 5 line 566; must be filed no later than 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end; recapture on line 221; renunciation under subsection 41(7) on or before 6 months after tax year-end).
New Brunswick ( New Brunswick Income Tax Act , Section 59, Schedule 360 / T2SCH360): 15% fully refundable (Schedule 5 line 597; recapture on line 573).

Newfoundland and Labrador ( Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador) , Section 42, Schedule 301 / T2SCH301 & Form T1129): 15% fully refundable (Schedule 5 line 520; Schedule 301 must be filed no later than 12 months after the filing due date; uniquely, NL eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance, except GST/HST input tax credits).

Yukon ( Income Tax Act (Yukon) , Schedule 442 / T2SCH442 & Form T1232): Provides a 15% fully refundable base R&D tax credit on eligible Yukon SR&ED expenditures, plus an additional 5% refundable credit on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (Schedule 5 line 698; Schedule 442 must be filed no later than 18 months after the end of the tax year).
