body.text: 8. Governing Bodies, Prescribed Filing Procedures, CRA Review Workflows, and Statutory Penalties
8.1 Strict Statutory Filing Deadlines (ITA Subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and Paragraph 127(9)(m))

Under subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is defined as 12 months after the income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations (T2): Income tax returns for corporations are generally due 6 months after the end of the taxation year; adding the 12-month period gives a total corporate SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the tax year-end.

Individuals / Sole Proprietorships (T1): The filing due date for individuals with self-employed business income is June 15 (5.5 months after the calendar year-end); adding the 12-month period gives a total individual SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the tax year-end.
Trusts (T3) and Partnership Members (T5013): Subject to reporting deadlines relative to their applicable income tax filing due dates plus 12 months.

body.text: Consequences of Late or Incomplete Filing: To meet SR&ED filing requirements, prescribed forms containing all prescribed information must be submitted on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline. As specified in the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy:

items: Filing Form T661 on time, but missing Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND): The claimant can include allowable SR&ED expenditures in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to reduce income, but cannot earn any Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on those expenditures.

Filing Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) on time, but missing Form T661 (or filing T661 late): The claimant cannot deduct any SR&ED expenditures or add them to the deductible pool, and cannot earn any ITC.

Partial Submissions / Missing Project Details: If a claim includes multiple projects (for example, 15 projects) but required project information in Part 2 of Form T661 is missing for some (for example, 5 projects) past the SR&ED reporting deadline, the CRA will not disallow the entire claim; the costs for the 5 incomplete projects will be disallowed, while the 10 complete projects filed on time will be accepted. (Note that claimants may choose to submit Part 2 project information for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value when filing, provided they complete and maintain Part 2 descriptions for all claimed projects at their place of business and submit them to the CRA upon request). Utilizing an existing balance from the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and Part 9 claim preparer information are not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline (though missing claim preparer information may incur penalties).

body.text: 8.2 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process via My Business Account. Pre-Claim Approval allows eligible businesses to have their proposed R&D projects evaluated to determine whether they qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before commencing work or incurring costs, within an 8-week determination timeline:

items: Step 1 — Request Initiation: A business opens a pre-claim approval request on Canada.ca and completes the form. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing with the CRA receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days; new SR&ED claimants are contacted by the CRA by phone within 5 business days.
Step 2 — Application Submission: The business completes the application and submits required documents via My Business Account.

Step 3 — Specialist Meeting (Within 4 Weeks): Within 4 weeks of submitting the application in My Business Account, a 2- to 5-hour meeting (in-person or virtual) with a CRA SR&ED specialist takes place. This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants, but may not be necessary for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing.
Step 4 — Pre-Claim Approval Determination (Within 8 Weeks): The business receives a pre-claim approval determination from the CRA within 8 weeks of submitting its application in My Business Account.

body.text: When the business subsequently files its SR&ED claim after year-end for projects granted Pre-Claim Approval, the CRA processes the claim under expedited review rules: if selected for review, the CRA may select the claim for an expenditure-only review and generally processes it within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim (unless the projects differ significantly from what was initially approved or additional unapproved projects are claimed).
8.3 The 13-Step Coordinated CRA Audit Process, Dispute Resolution, and Appeals

All filed SR&ED claims undergo risk assessment in the CRA's CORTAX and SR&ED Risk Management Tool systems. When a claim is selected for review, it is assigned to a dual-specialist team governed by the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (RTA) and the Financial Claim Review Manual for Financial Reviewers (FR) (which sets out a 13-step coordinated review workflow recorded in the CRA's AIMS and TF98 files and on Form T2020 memos, with T1 claims stored in Integras):

items: The Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Conducts the review of the work to determine whether it meets technical eligibility requirements. The RTA reports to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and may involve outside consultants or a CRA National Technology Sector Specialist (NTSS) with RTM approval. Per the RTA Manual, an RTA must not negotiate eligibility or expenditures, and must consult the RTM before recommending disallowance for lack of information, issuing unfavourable review decisions without conducting an on-site visit, issuing formal "Better Books and Records" letters (which include a Letter of Agreement / Undertaking to be signed and returned within 30 days, with a follow-up visit recommended after a minimum of 60 days), or when penalties or suspected fraud are identified. During on-site interviews, rough interview notes must be identified, dated, initialled, and retained in the TF98 file for potential examination by the Appeals Division, the Tax Court of Canada, or Quality Assurance.

The Financial Reviewer (FR): Reports to a Financial Review Manager (FRM) and reviews the expenditures and ITCs claimed. FRs must protect confidential information at the Protected B level, must not consent to audio or video recording by claimants, and must not sign non-disclosure agreements. In coordinated reviews, the RTA decides whether a contractor performed SR&ED or whether an employee was directly engaged in SR&ED, while the FR determines whether an individual is a "specified employee".

Proposal Package & 30-Day Representation Period: If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter summarizing proposed adjustments to expenditures, ITCs, and penalties, and detailed breakdowns. The claimant generally has 30 days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations.
Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution & Formal Notice of Objection: Under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns, disputes follow a three-step process:
Step 1: Talk directly with the reviewer(s) (RTA and/or FR);
Step 2: Talk with the reviewer's manager(s) (RTM and/or FRM);

Step 3: Request an Administrative Review after receiving the proposal package if concerns remain unaddressed. An Administrative Review is not a second technical or financial review of the claim by different reviewers; its aim is to verify that the review was conducted in compliance with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, and to confirm that the claimant was provided due process.

Formal Notice of Objection: If a claimant disagrees with the final CRA decision after the evaluation concludes, they have the right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 8.4 Statutory Penalties: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty and Subsection 163(2) Gross Negligence Penalty

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty — $1,000 Joint and Several Liability: Added to Form T661 following the 2013 federal budget announcements, Part 9 of Form T661 (lines 935–975) requires every claimant to attest whether a claim preparer was engaged in any aspect of preparing the claim, and to provide each claim preparer's name (line 940), Business Number (line 945; or Social Insurance Number collected under section 237 if an individual), billing arrangement code (line 950), billing rate (line 955), other billing arrangements (line 960), and total fee paid, payable, or expected to be paid (line 965). (If a claim preparer has confidentiality concerns, the claimant may use the Revised Optional Filing Measure for Part 9 by submitting a paper copy of Parts 1 and 9 directly to the tax centre at the same time the return is filed). If any prescribed information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, the SR&ED claim will not be disallowed, but a $1,000 penalty may be assessed, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (unless the claim preparer exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill of a reasonably prudent person).

Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (ITA Subsection 163(2)): Under subsection 163(2) (paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d)) and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), if a person knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: Penaltys. 163(2) = max($100, 0.50 × [Understated Part I Tax Payables. 163(2)(a) + Overstated Refunds. 163(2)(d)]) Under subsection 163(3), the burden of proof rests on the CRA to establish on a balance of probabilities ("more likely than not") that the false statement or omission was made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, rather than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act. Notably, per Section 4.3 of the CRA policy, when the gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC, the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund claimed, regardless of whether specific portions of the overstatement resulted from gross negligence or simple oversight.

body.text: 9. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

Because the CRA's administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts, disputes over SR&ED eligibility and expenditure qualification are governed by the jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Below is the analysis of the 13 foundational judicial precedents that govern Canadian R&D tax audits.
9.1 Foundational Eligibility and Statutory Interpretation Precedents

items: Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen , 97 DTC 724, [1997] 2 CTC 2846 (TCC): In Consoltex, Judge Bowman established the overarching canon of statutory interpretation for SR&ED provisions: because the tax incentives given for doing SR&ED are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada, the legislation dealing with such incentives must be given "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects".

Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen , 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC): Decided by Judge Bowman on May 1, 1998, Northwest Hydraulic is the foundational judicial precedent in Canadian SR&ED tax law. Evaluating physical hydraulic modelling projects (such as the Belleville Hydroelectric Project), Judge Bowman articulated the Five Questions framework. Key holdings include: (a) technological risk or uncertainty must be of a type that cannot be removed by "routine engineering or standard procedures" (techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field); (b) hypothesis formulation involves a five-stage process (observation of the subject matter, formulation of a clear objective, identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses, and methodical testing); (c) intuitive creativity or genius must operate within the total discipline of the scientific method; (d) a technological advance in Canada does not cease to qualify merely because a theoretical possibility exists that a researcher elsewhere (e.g., in China) made the same advance if that work is not generally known to competent professionals in the field; and (e) rejection of a hypothesis is still an advancement because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis.

Sass Manufacturing Limited v. Minister of National Revenue , 88 DTC 1363, [1988] TCJ No. 409 (TCC): Judge Sarchuk articulated the judicial definition of "systematic investigation", holding that Regulation 2900 requires an appellant to adduce cogent evidence of controlled experiments, highly accurate measurements, and the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence, including repeatable experiments in which the steps, the changes made, and the results are carefully noted—as opposed to unrecorded trial and error or routine engineering.

C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada , 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA): The Federal Court of Appeal formally approved and reiterated Judge Bowman's five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic as the governing appellate standard across Canada.

Tigney Technology Incorporated v. Her Majesty the Queen , Docket 95-2794(IT)G, January 9, 1997 (TCC): The Tax Court held that 33 or 34 experiments conducted temporarily in Kentucky, USA in November 1992 (because freshly harvested tobacco needed to be processed within two hours and was unavailable in Canada) did not constitute a separate and distinct systematic investigation, but formed an isolated and necessary component of the continuous scientific research centred in Edmonton, Canada. (Note: For post-2008 taxation years, foreign SR&ED employee salaries are additionally governed by the 10% permissible salary limit in subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)).

body.text: 9.2 Contemporaneous Documentation, Repeatability, and Expert Witness Precedents

items: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen , 99 DTC 5087, [1998] FCJ No. 1890 (FCA): In RIS-Christie, the Tax Court judge had found as a fact that an engineering uncertainty existed, a hypothesis was formulated, testing of models resolved the problem, and the taxpayer created a patented spatial membrane concrete forming panel embodying a technological advance, yet dismissed the appeal because the taxpayer lacked documentary test records enabling third parties to replicate the exact tests ("repeatability"). Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Robertson allowed the taxpayer's appeal with costs. Justice Robertson held that:

While documentary evidence showing the logical progression between tests is the "sure-fire way" to establish that research was systematic, third-party documentary repeatability is not an absolute statutory requirement.
Both documentary and oral (viva voce) evidence are admissible.

Where a project actually culminates in a proven technological advancement, it raises a rebuttable inference that the underlying testing and experimentation were carried out in a systematic manner according to Regulation 2900.

What constitutes "scientific research" under the Act is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the Court to decide, not expert witnesses, whose function is strictly limited to providing a "set of prescription glasses" through which technical facts may be viewed by the judge.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen , 2014 TCC 313: Allowing the appeal of a Montreal mechanical sub-assembler, Justice Jorré established three key audit defence principles:
Global Project Evaluation: Each project must be considered globally over the year, not each test individually.

No Statutory Mandate for Specific Contemporaneous Documents: Citing Salaison Lévesque Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 36 / 2014 FCA 296) and 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, Justice Jorré held that while the existence and content of contemporaneous documents are relevant to questions of fact and credibility, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific content, is not a condition for the scientific research or experimental development to be recognized." The CRA cannot impose obligations on taxpayers beyond what is required by the Act and Regulations.

Impartiality of CRA Expert Witnesses: Justice Jorré gave very little weight to the testimony of the CRA's scientific adviser appearing as an expert witness because there was confusion between his audit role (being guided by CRA policies and guidelines) and his courtroom role as an expert witness (providing an independent opinion based on personal expertise).

body.text: 9.3 Modern Appellate Precedents on Routine Engineering, the 2021 Guidelines, and Assistance

items: Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen , 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, 2012 DTC 5031: The Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that the criteria for determining whether a project qualifies as SR&ED are as set out in Northwest Hydraulic.

R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen , 2015 TCC 186, aff'd 2016 FCA 152: The Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and dismissed claims where work was done by trial and error by substituting raw materials or changing their concentration without a systematic scientific investigation.

Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen , 2017 TCC 6: Justice Sommerfeldt ruled in favour of the appellant on theatrical rigging development, noting that while there is no definitive statutory definition of "routine engineering", the term typically describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Crucially, Joel Theatrical demonstrated that a scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context and cannot be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedure.

Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada , 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246): The appellant argued that because the definition of SR&ED in the Income Tax Act does not explicitly contain the words "scientific method," the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic should not have been applied. Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Webb dismissed the appeal (with $1,670 costs), holding that under Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54 at para 10), Judge Bowman's criteria in Northwest Hydraulic properly interpret the statutory definition of SR&ED based on a textual, contextual, and purposive analysis, and have been repeatedly endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal.

National R&D Inc. v. Canada , 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47): In this software development appeal, the taxpayer argued that the CRA's 2021 SR&ED eligibility guidelines removed the requirement to follow the scientific method, and that the TCC erred in excluding its expert report. The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that:

The CRA's 2021 guidelines are not inconsistent with the Northwest Hydraulic test, did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method, and CRA administrative guidance is not binding on the courts in any event;
